title: Kling AI Camera Control: Master Push, Pull, Pan & Tilt in AI Video
claims: Vocabulary that Kling responds to: push in, pull back, pan left/right, tilt up/down, track forward, orbit slowly, static camera.
Give each shot one main camera action; stacking push, pan, tilt and zoom can make results unstable.
Do not pair contradictory instructions such as a static camera with an orbit.
Name a slow or steady speed; a note discouraging sudden motion can reduce erratic movement.
Pull-backs need a clear subject and an environment to reveal; pans confuse when the subject moves fast the other way; push-ins on fast subjects are hard to control.
notes: Vendor blog; results are probabilistic per the page.

title: Runway Gen-4.5: directing motion (image-to-video)
claims: For image-to-video describe change over time, not what the image already shows.
Direct subject and camera separately; if one should stay still, say so, otherwise the model tends to move both.
Most reliable move names: push-in, pull-back, pan, tilt, dolly, orbit, crane.
Add a pacing word (slow, gradual, subtle, rapid, continuous) or the move comes out generic.
Motion the frame cannot support (unseen body parts, contradicting the image state) is ignored or degraded. Durations offered: 5, 8 or 10 s.
notes: API aggregator documenting Runway Gen-4.5; not Runway itself.

title: Kling AI Camera Movement Prompts: A Director's Complete Reference
claims: Covers locked-off, push-in, pull-out, dolly, tracking, tilt, pan, handheld drift, crane, aerial and orbit with example wording.
Moves are set to about 5 s of travel; pans stay under roughly 30 to 45 degrees and orbits around 30 degrees per clip, never above 45.
Failure modes: two moves in one prompt, fast moves (warping), very wide or 360-degree orbits, dollies without foreground/midground/background depth (they read as zooms).
Claims 79% usable camera moves when five common mistakes are avoided versus 34% otherwise; this is the site's own unreplicated figure.
notes: Numbers are the author's own testing; treat as a rule of thumb.

title: 100 cinematic camera prompts you can copy
claims: Always include a speed word (slow, creeping, fast); the same orbit reads romantic when slow and frantic when fast.
Use one camera move per shot, two at most; three or more confuses the model.
A two-move combo works when one move leads into the other with a clear trigger moment.
Smooth predictable moves such as crane and aerial suit AI models; speed ramps work when the prompt names the moment the speed changes.
notes: Model rankings in the page are the author's opinion.

title: Runway Gen-4 guide: 5/10-second image-to-video prompts
claims: Write subject motion, camera motion, scene response and motion style, in that order; keep to one subject action and one camera move.
Treat each 5 or 10 s generation as one shot; combining a transformation, an orbit and a scene change makes motion compete.
Avoid negative instructions and do not list every visible object.
Cropping the source image to another aspect ratio can remove details before motion is made; fix composition in the image first.
When motion is wrong, simplify the prompt before changing the image; change one variable at a time.

title: Runway Gen-4 Turbo prompts
claims: To keep the camera still, state it positively, for example "Camera holds completely static".
Negative phrasing is not supported and describing an absence of movement can produce movement.
One scene and one primary action per generation; sequential actions or scene changes give inconsistent results.
Use 5 s for single actions and reveals, 10 s for longer or atmospheric shifts; lead with action verbs and pacing words.

title: The Ultimate Veo 3.1 Prompt Guide
claims: Write prompts like a shot list: subject and action, style, camera work, lighting and atmosphere, setting, technical specs.
Camera moves to request: slow pan, dolly-in, tracking, handheld, crane, whip-pan; shot types: establishing wide, push-in reveal, reaction, payoff, POV.
Name a lighting style (low-key, high-key, noir, motivated, backlight, haze) instead of "cinematic".
Clips are 4, 6 or 8 s; longer pieces are assembled from several clips in an editor like Flow.
Overloaded prompts and many characters are weak spots; start with one main character.
notes: The page contradicts itself on maximum length; the 4/6/8 s figure is the technical note.

title: How to Write Prompts That Work for Sora 2
claims: Open with camera angle and movement (low-angle tracking, descending overhead drone); say so if the camera should stay still because the model drifts subtly by default.
Describe light source and quality (side light with strong shadows, soft diffuse from above); specific stock or camera references beat the word "cinematic".
Keep clips roughly 5 to 10 s; consistency drifts longer, so edit short segments together.
Use precise verbs (sprinting, strolling) not "moving"; gentle motion like a scarf in a breeze beats storms and liquid collisions.

title: Sora 2 Prompting Guide (OpenAI Cookbook)
claims: Use one camera setup and one clear camera move per shot; one clear subject action per shot, written as small countable beats.
Shorter clips follow instructions more reliably; two 4 s clips stitched in editing may beat one 8 s clip.
Describe light quality and direction, name 3 to 5 palette colours and repeat them across shots.
Multi-shot prompts are possible if each shot block has its own camera, action and lighting; or generate shots standalone and edit.
Reuse identical wording for characters, wardrobe and lighting across shots; an image can anchor the first frame.
notes: Sora availability is reported as ending in 2026; the guidance still applies to other models in spirit.

title: AI video keeps adding cuts: a troubleshooting guide to one continuous shot
claims: Cuts appear when a prompt describes several moments; words such as "then", "cut to" and "reveals" signal a new beat or viewpoint.
Limit the prompt to one location, one main subject and one visible action; remove sequence and transition language.
State the camera plan separately: fixed shot, simple track or slow push-in, not several moves.
A cue like "one continuous shot from a fixed medium-wide camera angle" helps but does not guarantee the result.
Test one change at a time and log where the cut occurs.
notes: Redirected from veo3gen.app. No controlled tests.

title: What is the cut-hide technique in AI filmmaking?
claims: Separately generated clips rarely match exactly in light, background and colour; hide the seam by cutting during strong motion.
A still frame between two moving segments is the hardest place to hide a cut; cut on action.
Put strong foreground action opposite the seam region; correct the small colour gap with a slight curve adjustment.
With extension overlap, start the pick-up at about the third frame because the first frames often contain errors.

title: How do you maintain consistent lighting across multiple AI video shots?
claims: Set lighting rules once per project (sources, shadow colour, contrast) in a style document rather than per clip.
Keep a fixed lighting slot in every prompt and describe the light source concretely; colour-temperature drift is the commonest inconsistency.
Repeat one locked style block at the start of every prompt.
Chain clips by carrying the last seconds of one into the next, described as stronger than single-frame methods; apply one unified grade in post.

title: Every AI-generated shot invents its own light: how to keep lighting consistent
claims: Each clip is a stateless generation, so the model re-decides light direction, colour and quality every time; small rewordings cause visible change.
Define the light source in one sentence and reuse the exact wording in every shot of the scene; give colour temperature in Kelvin where accepted.
Light the widest shot first, then use that approved frame as a reference for closer shots.
Keep key-light direction consistent across angles and record source, direction, temperature in the scene plan.
Regenerating from a locked reference frame beats rewriting the prompt; check colour on full-size frames.

title: AI Video Lighting Prompts: Volumetric Light & Golden Hour
claims: Name source, direction, intensity and colour rather than vague words like "warm".
Reference colour temperatures: golden hour about 3000 to 3500 K, midday 5500 to 6500 K, tungsten about 3200 K; long shadows anchor time of day.
Atmosphere (haze, fog, dust) makes light beams visible; match light to material (soft for skin, hard for metal, backlight for glass).
In multi-shot scenes repeat the shared light source, mood and shadow direction in each shot.
Phrase guardrails positively (steady light, controlled highlights) instead of listing problems.
notes: Kelvin figures are conventional photography values, not model specs.

title: How to write AI video prompts
claims: Six-part prompt: subject, action, setting, camera movement, lighting, style.
Use only one camera move per clip; for complex movement generate separate shots and cut them together.
If movement is unpredictable, lock the camera as static; give the feel and duration of a move, such as a slow steady push-in.
Name the light source and quality (soft window light from one side, warm tone); avoid "good lighting".

title: Where Should Your Actor Look? Eyelines, Explained
claims: Keep the camera on one side of the line between two characters so each gaze points the same way from shot to shot.
Crossing the line reverses gaze directions and disorients the viewer.
If you must cross, use a neutral cutaway, or move the camera continuously across the line.
Use an establishing shot for group scenes and two- or three-shots to keep eyelines clear; map the lines while storyboarding.
Match eyeline height; looking down suggests authority, looking up vulnerability.

title: What is the 180-degree rule in film?
claims: The camera stays on one side of the imaginary line so each subject keeps the same left/right position.
Screen direction must carry across cuts: a car moving right to left should keep doing so in the next shot.
Crossing the line is a deliberate tool for unease; bend it with a neutral shot on the line, a visible camera move across it, or a cutaway.

title: Axis of Action (180-Degree Rule)
claims: The axis of action runs between two characters or along a subject's movement; the 180-degree rule keeps the camera on one side.
Filmmakers break it deliberately for horror, a shift of viewpoint, or to cheat the line in ensembles.
Crossing without a reason can make a moving subject seem to reverse direction.

title: Multi-scene AI video
claims: Plan the sequence first: storyboard, style guide with reference images and a shot plan with framing, movement and duration per scene.
Draw still frames of key moments first because fixing drift in a still is faster than in video.
Prompt template: fixed opening (style, mood), changing middle (the action), fixed closing (lighting, camera, format).
The strongest continuity method is using the last frame of one scene as the start image of the next.
Trim first and last frames to remove artifacts and grade to a common look; a transition fixes a bad edit point, regeneration fixes a bad scene.

title: Multi-shot AI video generator
claims: Single-shot tools make one continuous take; multi-shot output is several connected shots and needs a plan of how they relate.
Use a logical size progression (wide, medium, close-up, detail, back to wide); random angle jumps feel disjointed.
Give each shot the same fields: subject, action, location, camera, lighting, style, duration; one primary action each.
Keep sequences short because more cuts give more chances for continuity to break; carry the last frame forward.

title: How to create multi-cut cinematic AI videos
claims: A tool generates 3 to 5 shots for a 10 to 20 s video after writing a shot plan with camera positions, shot types and lighting notes.
Alternate wide shots (place) and close-ups (detail or emotion); follow shots track the subject.
Reviewing and editing the plan before generating is the cheap place to fix order, angles and lighting.
notes: Vendor tutorial for its own product.

title: Which AI video shot types fail most often?
claims: Multi-character contact shots, POV shots and over-the-shoulder shots are weak spots; reword rarely helps, change references or model.
Continuous one-take shots lose character, location and camera continuity at each segment boundary.
Dense fast-cut scenes overload the model; split them in two.
Plan about three generations per usable result.

title: Why is cutting on a still frame between AI-generated clips a problem?
claims: Cutting on a still frame exposes the seam because the eye scans a static image and finds small colour or lighting differences.
Choose edit points where both clips share movement.
Extension overlaps have bad first frames; usable action starts around frame three.
If a hold is needed, add a gentle camera move so motion carries the viewer across the join.

title: What is an establishing shot?
claims: An establishing shot opens a scene and shows where it takes place and how people relate to the surroundings.
Usually a wide or aerial view, it also sets tone and can signal time passing.
Start wide to set geography before moving closer; reuse the same location framing across scenes to show time passing.

title: Shot reverse shot
claims: Shot reverse shot puts the camera on one subject and then on the reverse view; common in dialogue, often over-the-shoulder.
By default match focal length, depth of field, camera movement and shot size across both setups; vary them only for meaning.
There is no single correct coverage; more setups give editing options.

title: Types of camera shot sizes in film
claims: Sizes from extreme wide (subject small, place emphasised) through full, medium wide (knees up), cowboy, medium (waist up), medium close-up (chest up), close-up, to extreme close-up.
Wide shots convey isolation or grandeur; close-ups reveal emotion; a medium shot works as a buffer before an emotional close-up.
Changing shot size creates contrast that signals a shift to the viewer.

title: Match cuts and types of cuts
claims: Match cuts join two scenes through a shared element: graphic match (shape, colour, composition), match on action, sound bridge, repeat cut.
Match on action carries a movement across two shots and gives momentum.
J-cuts and L-cuts overlap audio from one scene with the picture of the next.

title: What cinematic vocabulary terms improve AI video prompts?
claims: Name shot size, angle and movement first; then focal length, depth of field and exact aspect ratio.
Describe light by source, direction and contrast, not "warm"; replace "cinematic", "beautiful" with specific terms.
Recommends stating what must not appear because models drift to defaults (conflicts with Runway-style positive-only advice).
No benchmarks back the ranking of terms; examples are single productions.

title: Cinematic AI video prompts
claims: Push-in gives emotional emphasis, tracking gives momentum, handheld gives organic feel, orbit suits product reveals.
Low angle suggests authority, high angle vulnerability, tilted angle tension.
Sample prompts pair a move with a lens look, for example a slow push-in with shallow depth of field and an 85 mm lens look.
Change one element at a time and keep approved ones.
notes: Page does not cover clip duration.

title: The aspect ratio mistake that wastes 68% of your AI-generated video
claims: Cropping 16:9 (1920x1080) to 9:16 (608x1080) discards about 68% of horizontal pixels.
Match the reference image to the target ratio; a square image in a 16:9 tool makes the model invent edges.
Choose the final platform first and keep one ratio per sequence; generate natively for each platform.
Veo 3.1 reportedly supports native 9:16 output.
notes: Pixel arithmetic is checkable; the rest is the author's experience.

title: How does an editor control the rhythm of a film?
claims: Average shot length sets the audience baseline; many modern films sit around 4 to 6 s per shot.
Shorter shots raise tension, longer shots give calm; deviation from the baseline shapes mood.
Time cuts to emotional beats, even holding longer than seems necessary; long takes stay engaging through composition and movement.

title: Furious film editing: five films that average 2 seconds per shot
claims: Five films with about 2 s average shots and roughly 3000 shots each were played at 12x; only Mad Max: Fury Road stayed easy to follow.
Clear framing (viewer need not hunt for where to look) makes fast cutting readable; pointless fast cutting pulls viewers out.

title: How to create one-shot continuous videos with Seedance 2.0
claims: Plan the camera route (start, path, end) and the transition point for each change of scene, such as a doorway, corner, fog or focus shift.
Write the journey chronologically and state explicitly that the take has no cuts.
Physical transitions (doorways, curtains, stairs, fog) work more reliably than one environment morphing into another.
One generation runs up to 15 s; extensions add about 4 to 15 s; each extension prompt should restate the continuity.

title: Wan 2.2 Prompting Guide: image-to-video in 4 steps
claims: Image-to-video prompt: main movement, camera behaviour, lighting or weather, and speed or strength of motion.
Describe motion not appearance; animate only elements visible in the image.
Use concrete camera verbs (pans, zooms, sways, slow push-in, orbit); for a static camera say so explicitly.

title: How to avoid continuity errors in AI-generated videos
claims: Error types: identity, wardrobe/props, environment, lighting/colour, screen direction, temporal shimmer, camera perspective.
Storyboard first and last frame of each shot so they connect; map screen direction and lighting per shot; chain from the previous final frame.
For a big lighting jump (bright exterior to dark interior) generate an intermediate bridging clip.
Hide seams with cutaways, close-ups or environment shots; keep clips short and prompts templated.

title: How do I create static camera shots in Dream Machine?
claims: Ray2 drifts the camera slightly by default.
Opening the prompt with "still camera shot of" or "locked viewpoint of" is reported to keep the camera fixed.
notes: Page returned 404 to fetch; claims from search result text only.

title: How to Stop Unwanted Camera Motion in AI Prompts
claims: Recommends 'Static camera, locked shot' once; stacking 'stable', 'still', 'smooth' dilutes it. Keep prompts under 15 words with at most 2-3 motion keywords.
Claims a still source image cuts unwanted motion by 60-70% (internal numbers, not shared) and that drift sets in around 3.5 s, so keep the middle of a short clip.
Mechanical terms (tripod, locked-off) hold better than handheld, which adds randomness.

title: Stop unwanted camera movement in AI video
claims: Put a positive lock block first ('locked eye-level medium shot from one fixed tripod position'), then an exclusion list (zoom, push-in, pan, tilt, orbit, dolly, drift, reframing).
Write invariants: subject size stays constant, side seams and floor line stay put; leave about 10% padding around the widest movement; keep a walking subject free to leave the frame.
Diagnose by comparing first, middle, last frames: a subject that grows while the edges move out is a zoom; edges sliding together is a pan; bent lines with fixed anchors is background warp.

title: Firefly image to video keeps adding a slight push-in or pan
claims: A user reports that with every model in Firefly, the clip still gets a slight push-in or pan despite prompts forbidding zoom, pan, tilt and dolly, and asks for a true locked-camera mode.
A community expert's reply: negative prompts often do the opposite; state positively that the camera is fixed.

title: Image-to-video that actually moves, not just wiggles
claims: Too little motion: write a change (start state to end state, then hold), use committed verbs (open, turn, lift), drop 'subtly move', 'gently animate', 'drift', which give a wiggle; one action per shot.

Locked camera: state 'locked tripod shot (no camera movement)', give the primary motion to the subject, say the background stays static, avoid handheld words; orbit about 10 degrees keeps a subject centred.
notes: Original URL on veo3gen.app redirects here. Practitioner advice, untested claims.

title: Photo to video tips
claims: Name a static setup ('static shot', 'locked camera') even to keep the composition, because without it the model may add drift; a locked shot means the camera stays fixed and only subjects move.
One primary movement per clip, 5-10 s, prompts of 20-40 words; no numeric drift tolerance is given.
